title: More, most, and giving your opinion
title_target: กว่า ที่สุด คิดว่า — Kwàa, thîi-sùt, khít-wâa
goal: Compare two things, name the best of something, give your opinion, and disagree gently — the last piece you need before you can really hold a discussion.
bekal: comparing with กว่า and เท่ากับ
naming the "most" with ที่สุด
giving your opinion with คิดว่า and รู้สึกว่า
giving reasons with เพราะ and ก็เลย

dialogs.title: บทสนทนา — Choosing a place for a team meeting
dialogs.intro: Budi and Nok have a small debate about where to go. Notice that nobody says "you're wrong" — and yet the difference of opinion still comes across clearly.

lines.text: [พี่|Phîi][คิด|khít][ว่า|wâa][ร้าน|ráan][ไหน|nǎi][ดี|dii][กว่า|kwàa][คะ|khá]
lines.id: Phi, which restaurant do you think is better?
lines.literal: older-sibling — think — that — shop — which — good — more — (polite)?

lines.text: [ชั้น|Chán][บน|bon][เงียบ|ngîap][ค่ะ|khâ] [จอง|Jaawng][ชั้น|chán][บน|bon][ก็ได้|kâw-dâai][ค่ะ|khâ]

lines.speaker: บูดี:
lines.text: [ดี|Dii][เลย|loei][ครับ|khráp] [งั้น|Ngán][ตกลง|tòk-long][ตาม|taam][นี้|níi][ครับ|khráp]
lines.literal: good — really — (polite). in-that-case — agree — according-to — this — (polite).

notes: **กว่า kwàa = "more, -er", and it comes AFTER the adjective.** *ดีกว่า* (better), *แพงกว่า* (more expensive), *ใกล้กว่า* (closer). To name what you're comparing with, put it after: *ร้านนี้แพงกว่าร้านนั้น* (this place is more expensive than that one).

**ที่สุด thîi-sùt = "most, -est", also after the adjective.** *อร่อยที่สุด* (tastiest), *ไกลที่สุด* (farthest). Thai has no special forms like English "-est" or "best" — just one word added, and it works for every adjective without exception.

**เท่ากับ thâo-kàp = "equal to".** *ราคาเท่ากัน raa-khaa thâo-kan* (the same price). For "not equal": *ไม่เท่ากัน*. Notice the word *เท่า thâo*, which also appears in *เท่าไหร่* (how much) — same root: "how much, as much".

**คิดว่า khít-wâa = "think that", the standard way to give an opinion.** A shorter, very common form is **…ว่า… wâa** on its own — *ผมว่าใกล้สำคัญกว่า* (I'd say being close matters more). This short form sounds natural and relaxed.

**รู้สึกว่า rúu-sùek-wâa = "feel that"**, and it's softer than *คิดว่า*. Raising an objection with *รู้สึกว่า* makes it sound like a personal impression, not a judgment — and that's exactly right in Thailand.

**เห็นด้วย hěn-dûai = "agree"**, literally "see with". Its negative is *ไม่เห็นด้วย* (disagree) — but ⚠️ that sounds quite blunt in a Thai meeting. A softer form: *อาจจะ…ก็ได้นะครับ/คะ àat-jà … kâw dâai ná* ("maybe … could work too"), which suggests without rejecting.
**เพราะ phráw = "because", and ก็เลย kâw-loei = "so, that's why".** Together they link cause and effect: *ฝนตก ก็เลยมาสาย* (it rained, so I was late), *มาสายเพราะฝนตก* (I was late because it rained).
**แค่ khâae = "only, just".** *แค่ชั่วโมงเดียว* (just one hour), *แค่นี้* (just this much). It's also a common sign-off: *แค่นี้นะ khâae níi ná* — "that's all for now".

after: **ดีกว่า has a very useful second meaning: "it'd be better to…"** — a suggestion. *ไปเช้าดีกว่า* = we'd better leave early. *ไม่ไปดีกว่า* = maybe better not to go. It's one of the gentlest ways to suggest something in Thai.

grammars.title: Giving opinions, agreeing, disagreeing

head: Thai
Pronunciation
Meaning
Tone

เห็นด้วยครับ/ค่ะ
จริงครับ/ค่ะ
ก็จริงนะครับ/คะ
อาจจะ…ก็ได้

after: ⚠️ **Disagreeing in Thai almost always starts with an acknowledgment.** Watch Budi in the dialogue: he says *อ๋อ งั้นก็จริงครับ* (oh, that's true too) before putting forward his own view. This order — acknowledge first, then speak — is the key to discussing without making anyone lose face.

head: Thai
Pronunciation
Meaning
Position
rows: เพราะ / เพราะว่า

blocks.text: An example using both at once: *เมื่อวานฝนตกหนัก ก็เลยมาสายครับ ขอโทษที่ไม่ได้โทรมาบอกครับ* — it rained hard yesterday, so I was late. Sorry I didn't call to let you know.

blocks.title: ก็ — the smallest, most frequent word
items: *ก็ kâw* shows up in almost every sentence of Thai conversation, and its meaning shifts with its position: "also" (*ผมก็ไป* — I'm going too), "then" (*ถ้าฝนตกก็ไม่ไป* — if it rains, then I won't go), and "well" as a softener (*ก็ดีนะ* — well, it's not bad).
You don't need to master all of them now. Just know that this tiny word works hard — and that hearing it mid-sentence is normal, not a sign you've missed something.

blocks.title: Three sentences that make you sound mature in a meeting
items: **ผม/ฉันคิดว่าน่าจะดีกว่านะครับ/คะ** — I think that would probably be better. Softener stacked on softener, and that's exactly what makes it sound seasoned.
**เข้าใจครับ/ค่ะ แต่ผม/ฉันรู้สึกว่า…** — I understand, but I feel… Acknowledge first, then speak.
**งั้นตกลงตามนี้นะครับ/คะ** — so we're agreed on this, then. A closing line that sums up the decision without sounding pushy.
